checks.context: A single-region trail misses all API activity in other regions, including global services like IAM. Attackers often operate in regions you don't monitor. Always create multi-region trails.

checks.message: Log file integrity validation not enabled
checks.context: Without integrity validation, you cannot prove that CloudTrail logs haven't been tampered with after delivery. This is required for forensic investigations and many compliance frameworks.

checks.message: CloudTrail logs not encrypted with KMS
checks.context: Encrypting CloudTrail logs with a KMS key ensures that only authorized principals can read your audit logs. Without encryption, anyone with S3 read access to the bucket can read all API activity.

checks.message: Global service events excluded — IAM activity will not be logged
checks.context: IAM, STS, and CloudFront are global services. Using --no-include-global-service-events means all IAM API calls (CreateUser, AttachRolePolicy, AssumeRole, etc.) are invisible in this trail. This is a critical audit gap because IAM activity is exactly what attackers try to hide.

checks.message: Disabling multi-region trail. API activity in other regions will be invisible
checks.context: A single-region trail misses all API activity in other regions, including IAM. Attackers often operate in regions you don't monitor.
Without integrity validation, you cannot prove that CloudTrail logs haven't been tampered with. This is required for forensic investigations and compliance.

checks.message: Excluding global service events, so IAM activity will not be logged
checks.context: IAM, STS, and CloudFront are global services. Excluding them means all IAM API calls are invisible in this trail.

checks.message: Stopping CloudTrail logging creates an audit blind spot
checks.context: Disabling CloudTrail is one of the first actions taken by attackers after gaining access. All API activity during the logging gap will be unrecorded. This action itself will be the last event logged.

checks.message: Deleting a CloudTrail trail permanently removes audit logging
checks.context: Deleting a trail stops all logging immediately. This is a common attacker technique to cover tracks. Ensure you have an alternative logging mechanism before deleting, and investigate why this deletion is needed.

checks.message: CloudWatch log group not encrypted with KMS
checks.context: Log groups containing sensitive application data, VPC flow logs, or CloudTrail logs should be encrypted with a KMS key. Without encryption, anyone with CloudWatch Logs read access can view all log data.

checks.message: Log group deletion permanently removes all log data
checks.context: Deleting a CloudWatch log group destroys all log streams and events within it. This data cannot be recovered. Ensure logs are exported to S3 or archived before deletion if retention is required.

checks.message: Verify retention period meets your compliance requirements
checks.context: Many compliance frameworks (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) require log retention of 1-7 years. Setting a short retention period may cause you to fail audits or lose evidence needed for incident investigations.
Deleting a log stream removes all events within it. If this stream contains security-relevant logs (VPC flow logs, application errors, access logs), ensure they are archived before deletion.

checks.message: Verify the log group has appropriate retention and KMS encryption configured
checks.context: Log streams inherit the log group's retention and encryption settings. If the log group has no retention policy, logs are kept indefinitely, increasing storage costs and compliance exposure.

checks.message: Verify the metric filter pattern is specific enough to avoid false positives
checks.context: Overly broad filter patterns can generate excessive CloudWatch metrics and trigger false alarms. Overly narrow patterns miss real events. Test the pattern against sample log data first.

checks.message: Verify the resource policy does not grant PutLogEvents to untrusted accounts
checks.context: A CloudWatch Logs resource policy controls which services and accounts can write to your log groups. A permissive policy allows attackers to inject false log entries or fill your log groups with junk data.
